summary: Specifies the Daytime service, which sends the current date and time as a character string without regard to the input. It is an Internet Standard for hosts that choose to implement it.

plainLanguage.summary: The Daytime Protocol returns the current date and time as readable text. It works over TCP or UDP, and the RFC points to a different protocol for time data intended for machines.

questions: what port does the daytime service use
subtitle: Defines a service that returns the current date and time as text.

tldr.problem: A simple service is useful for asking a host for the current date and time in a human-readable form.
tldr.mechanism: A server on port 13 sends a date-and-time string over TCP or returns one in response to a UDP datagram, ignoring the input.
tldr.outcome: The RFC recommends a one-line ASCII response and points readers to the Time Protocol when machine-usable time is needed.

today: RFC 867 is listed as an Internet Standard in the unit metadata. The metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: A Readable Date and Time
sections.content: The Daytime service sends the current date and time as a character string without regard to the input. The RFC describes it as a useful debugging and measurement tool for hosts that choose to implement it.
sections.plainLanguage: The service tells a client the current date and time in text. It does not interpret the data sent to it.

sections.title: TCP and UDP Services
sections.content:
For TCP, a server listens on TCP port 13. After the connection is established, it sends the current date and time as an ASCII string, ignores received data, and closes the connection.

For UDP, the server listens on UDP port 13. Each incoming datagram receives an answering datagram with the current date and time as an ASCII string.
sections.plainLanguage: Over TCP, the server sends the time and then closes the connection. Over UDP, each request gets one datagram containing the time.

sections.title: Writing the Time
sections.content:
The RFC defines no specific format for the date and time. It recommends ASCII printing characters, spaces, carriage return, and line feed, and recommends that the response fit on one line.

The memo gives two popular text formats and says to use the Time Protocol, RFC 868, when a machine-usable time value is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The response is meant for people to read, and the RFC does not require one exact date format. For time that a program can use directly, the memo points to the Time Protocol.

references.text: Time Protocol, RFC 868, referenced for machine-usable time.
